title: Would you do an ‘influencer degree’?
description:
It’s no surprise more people want to become influencers - a study found that in 2024, YouTube content creators alone contributed £2.2bn to the UK’s economy. But… would you pay thousands to study how to be one?

A growing number of universities around the world, like Arizona State University in the US, have started offering Content Creation courses. We hear from Martyna who is currently studying BA Content Creation at Nottingham Trent University in the UK.

So are these courses the best way to become an influencer? Or are they more about training to go into a career in online marketing?

BBC journalist Megan Lawton takes us through the stats and Daanish (@doctordaanish), a medical doctor and influencer, gives us his take on these degrees.

Instagram: @bbcwhatintheworld Email: whatintheworld@bbc.co.uk WhatsApp: +44 330 12 33 22 6 Presenter: Hannah Gelbart Producers: William Lee Adams and Chelsea Coates Video Producer: Tim Hodges Editor: Emily Horler
summaryZh: 本集 BBC 節目《What in the World》探討大學開設內容創作與網紅學位的趨勢，以及這類課程是否值得投入時間與高額學費。節目採訪了正在英國諾丁漢特倫特大學攻讀內容創作學位的學生 Martyna 表示，課程核心主要為數位行銷、媒體研究與作品集建立，而非僅是教人如何成為網紅。 BBC 記者 Megan Lawton 指出，雖然創作者經濟規模龐大，但多數創作者收入偏低，這類學位提供的行銷技能與法律知識有助於提升就業競爭力。不過，醫師兼創作者 Daanish 則認為，相關技巧皆可透過網路自學，學生不應為了缺乏就業保證的學位而背負債務。
summaryEn: This episode of BBC's What in the World explores the rise of university degrees in content creation and considers whether they are worth the financial investment. Student Martyna, currently studying BA Content Creation at Nottingham Trent University, explains that her course focuses heavily on digital marketing, media studies, and portfolio building rather than simply teaching students how to become famous influencers. BBC journalist Megan Lawton provides context on the rapidly growing creator economy and notes that while many individual creators earn low incomes, these degrees aim to equip students with transferable marketing and legal skills. Conversely, medical doctor and content creator Daanish argues against pursuing such degrees, advising aspiring creators to learn skills online for free rather than accumulating debt for a degree with no guaranteed career outcome.

vocabulary.example: And is it worth potentially getting into debt for?
Every big brand, every small brand that you see has a social media presence, and there is a whole group of people working behind that.
I think you can definitely teach confidence.
And I've been reading a little bit of criticism that these content creation degrees have been getting, and I hear that you want to use yours for digital marketing.
How many universities are offering degrees like this, and are they getting more popular?

This is an interesting stat, that nearly half of people who consider themselves content creators make under $15,000 US a year, so that's not money to be sniffed at, but at that point, that is not your main source of income.
Well, this morning I went onto the UCAS website, which is essentially the UK's directory of courses offered, typed in content creation, and 149 options came up.
I think if you're going to do a degree, you should only do one that actually gets you the job or the outcome that you want and has a bit of a guarantee attached.
Don't go into so much debt thinking that this degree is going to teach you something that isn't already accessible on the internet.
I think what they would more tell you to think about is in this job landscape, what skill sets are necessary, and is that £30,000 that I'm going to spend going to make me more employable?

phrases.example: Some of them are absolutely killing it.

But some people say that being an influencer isn't a real job, the amount of debt that you might rack up from doing this degree isn't actually worth it when you can learn a lot of these skills for yourself online.
So I feel that universities are really just catering to this career path.
She was creative, had an eye for shooting content, but didn't actually know how it kind of boiled down when it came to working with brand deals.

So Megan, if you're someone who is thinking about whether they want to go and spend three years of their life and possibly tens of thousands of dollars or pounds on a degree like this, what are the things that they should be weighing up?

vocabulary.example: So if you could get a degree in content creation, what would your job prospects be like?
Being an influencer, it's about personality, confidence, charisma.
So I feel that universities are really just catering to this career path.
Goldman Sachs, for example, they valued it last year, this is globally, at $250 billion US, and they project that by next year, that's going to reach 480 billion.

And I think actually, you spoke about Arizona University, I've spoken with Nottingham Trent University, I know Martina's part of that course, and Jackie Gersch, she runs the course, she was saying there are very few people, which kind of echoes what Martina said, on that course who want to be influencers.

vocabulary.meaningZh: 極其重要的、不可或缺的
vocabulary.example: The majority of them are there because they want to pick up these digital marketing skills, which in the job landscape, no matter if you want to be in front of camera, beside camera, in a business, so many of these skills are now vital for so many different industries.

And people listening to this might think it's actually really good if someone wants to become a content creator that they have thought about the ethics of content creation, and they have thought about media law and what is and isn't legal to post because people who are self-taught might not actually know about a lot of that stuff.

One content creator who's been around for about 15 years, her name's Aisha Beasley, she's based in Arizona, and she said had the course have been offered back when she was starting 10-15 years ago, she would have signed up for it, because one of the things she struggled with most is the monetizing of things.
Don't go into so much debt thinking that this degree is going to teach you something that isn't already accessible on the internet.
